There is a story reported by Asellio which is a good example of the treatment of dependent people by a Roman. Crassus was preparing to besiege Leucae, which we must suppose that Aristonicus had seized again. He wanted a large piece of timber for a battering-ram, and he wrote to a master-builder of Elaea, a town friendly to the Romans,to send the larger of two pieces of timber which Crassus had seen there.The builder knowing the purpose for which the timber was wanted did not send the larger piece, but he sent the smaller, which he considered to be more suitable for the purpose,and it was of course more portable. Crassus summoned the man to his presence, and without any regard to the reasons which were alleged for sending the smaller piece, he ordered him to be stripped and whipped well on the ground that the authority of a commander would be ruined, if a man should not exactly obey orders and should use his own judgment.

Talk about an anecdote! I first found this story in Robert Greene's 48 Laws of Personal Power. The stories there tend a bit weakly cited, but that version does include a moral lesson. Greene reports the tale about Publius Crassus Dives Mucianus, aka "Mucianus". I wondered about this story and found George Long's Decline of the Roman Republic. More importantly, Long claims that the builder did NOT know the purpose of the request. (The moral is built on that exchange.) Which version is correct? Perhaps we could consult Asellio (sometimes I do such things), but what guarantee do we have Asellio got it right?

This is an excellent question. I'll try to do my best to answer it.

The key elements of language are comprehension, repetition, fluency, naming, reading and writing. Any disorder in any element of language is called aphasia. The medical name for the 'slurring' in language people experience when they get drunk is aphasia. Language is produced in the dominant cerebral hemisphere (that is, if you are right-handed, in the left hemisphere) with the involvement of two principal areas:

-Wernicke area or language comprehension area. This area is responsible for the production of language and the comprehension of it. A patient with a stroke in this area won't be able to understand what you tell him and when he speaks he will speak pure nonsense; however, they are unaware of this.

-Broca area or motor speech area. It receives the input from Wernicke area through the arcuate fasciculus and is responsible for the production of speech. This is responsible for the coordination of the muscles of speaking and the thought process of speaking. Damaging this area produces a telegraphic speech and the patient is irritated by his inability of expressing himself.

In deaf people, although the precise location of language comprehension and motor sign areas has not yet been established (or at least I couldn't find anything), the mechanism of language production is the same. Now, the cognitive impairment during alcohol ingestion is due to the accumulation of acetaldehyde, a metabolite of alcohol. This accumulation affects the whole brain, so the aphasia produced is both an expressive (Broca) and receptive (Wernicke) aphasia, in which the person has not only problems understanding the language but also trying to speak (or to sign).

So basically, the answer is yes.
